Goethe says in 1824 — Not in the edition by Hesse cited there, but in J. W. Goethe, Sämtliche Werke nach Epochen seines Schaffens (Munich edition), vol. 13/1, Munich 1992, p. 403.
Stahl-Jolson as early as 1840 — Refers to Friedrich Julius Stahl, Die Kirchenverfassung nach Lehre und Recht der Protestanten, Erlangen 1840.
sbirreria — Refers to the work of the sbirri, judicial and police officers in the Papal States who were militarily organized and armed.

Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Francis Bacon, Fr. Baconi De Verulamio Sermones fideles, Ethici, Politici, Œconomici: Sive Interiora Rerum. Accedunt Faber Fortunæ Colores Boni Et Mali …, Leiden 1644. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 no. 23412.
The passage is not actually on p. 246, but on p. 240:

Cardinales Romani, (qui Theologi sunt, & Fratres & Scholastici,) verbum usurpant, extremi contemptus & convitii, erga negotia Civilia: Vocant enim negotia Civilia, (velut, Belli, Legationum, Iudiciorum, & hujusmodi,) Hispanico vocabulo, Sbirrarias; quod sonat, Munera Lictorum & Scribarum.

“The Roman cardinals, who are theologians, friars, and scholars, use a term of extreme contempt and disdain for civil affairs. They call such matters—war, diplomacy, judicial affairs, and the like—by the Spanish expression sbirreria, meaning work fit for bailiffs and clerks.”

Otto Weininger claims … — Schmitt quotes from his copy of the following edition, inscribed “Carl Schmitt, Düsseldorf, May 1912”: Otto Weininger, Über die letzten Dinge, with a biographical foreword by Moritz Rappaport, 3rd ed., identical to the 2nd, Vienna et al. 1912, pp. 83 ff.
draft of a project — See BW Mohler, p. 105.
If the religious laws of the Roman emperors … — Correctly: “Without the imperial legislation from Constantine through Theodosius, the Greco-Roman religion would still be alive today.”
Jacob Burckhardt, Weltgeschichtliche Betrachtungen (Kröner Taschenausgabe, 55), Stuttgart 1978, p. 57.
“Blind morsel arches without coarseness …” — R. M. Rilke, poem “Vasen-Bild (Toten-Mahl).” In: idem, Späte Gedichte, Leipzig 1934, p. 128. See Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 293–94; BW Mohler, pp. 104–5.
“Everything here will find …” — Quotation from the poem “Die kleine Schöpfung” by Konrad Weiß. In: Weiß, p. 384:

The farmer came home with his hand, stopped and properly took his stand before our three travelers there, and asked: Child, companion, where are you from, where are you going, where is your home? The rooster said: All this will find its place within, and speak from the mind.

“The magnificent sentences in the Phenomenology of Spirit” — In the Moldenhauer and Michel edition of Hegel’s works, Frankfurt am Main 1970, the quotations can be found in vol. 3, pp. 365, 138, and 144.
“The subject-object steamroller rolls …” — See also Schmitt’s ballad “Die Sub-stanz und das Sub-jekt.” In: Civis, 9 June 1955, pp. 29–30; now also in: Gedichte, pp. 16–21.
“Let them mock us, so long as they spare us their pity.” — Walter Warnach, Die Welt des Schmerzes, Pfullingen 1952, p. 111.
amor amaritudinis — “love of bitterness.” Used here as the opposite of amor fati, love of one’s necessary fate, in which Nietzsche saw human greatness.
Peripsema — “scum”; see above, note to p. 23.
Congrua — the minimum income guaranteed to a clergyman from the revenues of his benefice.

“The terror no one dares to name” — See C. Schmitt, “Gesang des Sechzigjährigen.” In: ECS, pp. 92–93; now in: Gedichte, pp. 5–7. Schmitt explains what he meant by this terror in the entry for 7 October 1951.

“A work by Montlosier” — François Dominique de Reynaud de Montlosier (1755–1835), French politician and opponent of ultramontanism. The work quoted was published not in 1826 but in 1827: F. D. de R. de Montlosier, Les Jésuites, les Congrégations et Le parti prêtre en 1827. Mémoire a M. le comte de Villèle …, Paris 1827, p. 65:

“I am well aware that there is a large class of people who do not want anyone concerning themselves with priests. For such people, religion is of no importance, and priests are of no more importance than religion. Their doctrine is this: criticize nothing the priests do, and believe nothing they say.”

“The word of thinkers has no authority. The word of thinkers has no authors in the sense in which writers have authors. The word of thinking is poor in images and without charm. The word of thinking rests in a sobering return to what it says.”
Martin Heidegger, Gesamtausgabe, vol. 7, section 1, Frankfurt am Main 2000, p. 234.
“Poor in deeds and rich in thoughts” — See above, note to p. 127.
“Gliding on sultry dactyls …” — Published in: Die neue Gesellschaft. Bemerkungen zum Zeitbewußtsein, ed. Rüdiger Altmann and Johannes Gross, Stuttgart 1958, p. 99. Now also in: Gedichte, p. 26.

“We arrive at the way we behave more by acting against ourselves than by acting out of ourselves.” — Quotation from Ludwig Raiser (1904–1980), jurist. In the Deutsche Universitätszeitung (1951, no. 9, p. 7), Raiser published an article entitled “Carl Schmitt — kein Bundesgenosse” (“Carl Schmitt — No Ally”).
“all righteous comb-makers” — See above, note to p. 41.
“I am trying to bring the accident of my own present into order through pure thought.” — See Schmitt’s letter to G. Jünger, 24 February 1948:

“I do not think about the future, because I know how powerless we are. Nor do I seek the past, because I do not want, by reflecting on myself, to outlive myself. So what am I looking for, and what am I doing? I am trying to bring the accident of my own present into order through pure thought.”
BW GJ, p. 105. Schmitt wrote something similar to E. R. Huber on 2 June 1948; BW Huber, p. 322. See also above, p. 73.
ἀναγκαζόμενος — See above, note to p. 18.

Rud. Fischer — Rudolf Fischer (1900–1961), journalist, who publicly but anonymously defended Schmitt. See X [= R. Fischer], “Hexenverfolgung. Der Fall Carl Schmitt. Charaktermord.” In: Der Fortschritt, 25 January 1952; see BW Mohler, pp. 115–16, 119; BW Forsthoff, pp. 84, 387.

Don Capisco (et obmutesco) — When Jünger criticized Schmitt for his conduct in 1933, Schmitt replied on 5 February 1950 with the sentence: “Capisco et obmutesco” — “I understand and fall silent.” BW EJ, p. 248. He later responded in the same way to criticism from Nicolaus Sombart; see Schmitt’s letter to Sombart of 7 January 1978, BW Sombart, p. 129.
“namesake of Carlo Schmid” — See above, note to p. 52.

V. Leemans — Victor Leemans (1901–1971), social scientist and politician, author of Carl Schmitt. Bijdrage tot de sociologie van Staat en Politiek, Antwerp 1933; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 28380.
“This outward element initially makes the inward visible only as an organ, or gives it a being for others at all; for the inward, insofar as it is in the organ, is the activity itself.”
G. W. F. Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes. In: idem, Werke, vol. 3, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, Frankfurt am Main 1970, pp. 234–35.

The character assassination as one of the fine arts — A reference to Thomas De Quincey, On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts, 1827 and later editions. See also the caption to the illustration on p. 257.
“to Mohler, 12 November” — See BW Mohler, p. 108.

Lilian Winstanley — The English author Lilian Winstanley (1875–1960) made one of the first attempts, in her 1921 book Hamlet and the Scottish Succession, to interpret Shakespeare’s Hamlet against the political and historical background of the Elizabethan period. The book was translated into German by Anima Schmitt as L. Winstanley, Hamlet, Sohn der Maria Stuart, Pfullingen 1952. Carl Schmitt wrote a substantial foreword.

“to M. F.” — In his history of the English Revolution, Die große Revolution in England (1951), Michael Freund portrays James I as a grotesque figure. Schmitt commented on this in a letter to Freund dated 7 March 1953; RW 265 no. 13003. In March 2015, the antiquarian-book market ZVAB listed a copy of the 1956 edition of Hamlet oder Hekuba bearing a dedication to M. Freund.
Forrestal — James Vincent Forrestal (1892–1949), United States Secretary of Defense. Doubts were raised about whether his death was really suicide.

“Rest. Board at Herford” — The “Restitution Board” was an international court that decided claims for restitution arising from the period 1933–1945. It existed from 1955 to 1990 and was based in Herford until 1984. Schmitt must therefore have added this entry later, something also suggested by the different handwriting.
“Smend wrote this to me as early as 1938” — This refers either to Smend’s letter of 10 July 1938 or to a letter that has been lost; see BW Smend, pp. 99–100, note 333.
“the passages on p. 86 of my Leviathan” — Schmitt means Hobbes’s distinction between an outward “profession of the tongue” and inward belief, which Spinoza transfers from religion to philosophy:

“Only a few years after the publication of the Leviathan, the first liberal Jew fixed his attention on this barely visible fracture. He immediately recognized it as the great point through which modern liberalism could break in, and from which the entire relationship Hobbes had established and intended between outward and inward, public and private, could be turned into its opposite. Spinoza carried out this reversal in the famous chapter 19 of his Tractatus theologico-politicus, published in 1670.”
Bakunin: il n’y a rien de plus borné … —

“Germany itself, moreover, cured me of the philosophical disease that prevailed there. After looking more closely into metaphysical problems, it did not take me long to become convinced of the emptiness and vanity of all metaphysics. I looked for life in it, but found only death and boredom. I looked for action, but found nothing but absolute inactivity. This discovery was greatly helped by my personal relations with German professors, because there is nothing more narrow-minded, more contemptible, or more ridiculous than the German professor — or the German in general!”
M. Bakounine, Confession (1857), reissue of the edition published in 1932, Paris 2001, pp. 61–62.

“Although, for example, the Roman people once governed the land of Judaea through a governor, Judaea was not therefore a democracy, because the people were not governed by an assembly that every one of them had a right to enter; nor was it an aristocracy, because they were not governed by an assembly that any elected person among them might enter.”
Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, trans. Jutta Schlösser, ed. Hermann Klenner, Hamburg 1996, p. 163.

Ceterum censeo Romam esse liberandam (a Romanitate) — “For the rest, I believe that Rome must be liberated — from Romanness.” A variation on the famous sentence with which Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches in the Senate:
“For the rest, I believe that Carthage must be destroyed.”

Eulenburg Affair — The dispute between Philipp, Prince of Eulenburg-Hertefeld, and the journalist Maximilian Harden. Harden accused the circle around Eulenburg, which exercised considerable influence over the Kaiser, of homosexuality, and the affair grew into a major public scandal.

“Parallel: Kortner — W. Krauss” — The director Fritz Kortner considered Werner Krauss a great actor, but reproached him for his closeness to National Socialism. Schmitt said that he had once met Krauss on a train and spoken with him.

“A professor, who was also a State Councillor, I think his name was Schmidt!” — From a note by Colonel General Werner von Fritsch dated 1 February 1938 concerning the Blomberg Affair, which led to his removal as commander-in-chief of the Army:

“In the autumn, the Party once again intensified its campaign against me. It was driven above all by the Gestapo and related circles. They succeeded in largely convincing Göring that I was planning a coup. Himmler claimed to know that this coup would be carried out on 10(?) January 1935, or on some other day in January 1935. For this reason, Blomberg invited the commanding generals and many other senior officers to an evening of beer at the Kaiser Wilhelm Academy on the first date in question, I believe 10 January 1935. Himmler gave a lecture.

“The incriminating point against me was supposedly that I had invited a professor, who was also a State Councillor, I think his name was Schmidt, to give a lecture on constitutional law on a Thursday at the Tirpitzufer. Göring claimed that the lecture was intended to prove that a coup was permissible under constitutional law. In the presence of the minister and numerous officers!
“The invitation had been issued by Department 4. The man was and remains completely unknown to me. The lecture was cancelled.”
Friedrich Hoßbach, Zwischen Wehrmacht und Hitler 1934–1938, 2nd rev. ed., Göttingen 1965, p. 61.
“We are not afraid of the danger of what has been called a ‘judicialized politics,’ which the namesake of our colleague Carlo Schmid — whose name is spelled with two t’s — has painted on the wall.”

“The Jew has emancipated himself in a Jewish manner, not only by acquiring the power of money, but because through him, and also without him, money has become a world power, and the practical Jewish spirit has become the practical spirit of the Christian peoples. The Jews have emancipated themselves to the extent that the Christians have become Jews.”
K. Marx, “Zur Judenfrage.” In: Marx/Engels, Werke, vol. 1, Berlin 1971, p. 373.
Blasius blessing — On 3 February, the feast day of St. Blaise, this blessing is given by holding two consecrated candles in the form of a St. Andrew’s cross before the face and throat.
“everything becomes a set of brass knuckles in his hands” — An allusion to Gerhard Nebel’s boxing career and his fights; see above, p. 242.

Drath & Leibholz — The constitutional lawyer Martin Drath (1902–1976) dealt critically with Schmitt in his unpublished habilitation thesis at Jena in 1946. In 1951 he became a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court. See van Laak, pp. 166 ff.
